summary: Static, design-level study of 6,003 public n8n workflow templates that include LLM nodes. RQ1 labels the primary LLM task with deepseek-v4-flash (96% agreement on 200 manual labels; keyword and NLI baselines 40.5% and 14.5%). RQ2 classifies graph topology (23.27% linear, 22.32% branch/merge, 18.92% cyclic, 18.74% multi-component). RQ3 finds 1,829 workflows with any platform error handling, 684 traceable to LLM outputs, mostly node-local settings (retry_on_fail, on_error_control). RQ4 traces LLM-to-external-action paths: 41.80% logic-gated, 26.52% direct, 2.78% human-gated. Ten findings and five takeaways; no runtime execution or outcome data.

claims.claim: LLM workflows are structurally diverse; only 23.27% are strict linear chains.
claims.evidence: Static graph analysis of n8n JSON (Table 1, §3.3). The four named categories sum to 83.25%; the remaining 16.75% is not explained. 'Cyclic' (18.92%) is not separated into item loops vs retry/repair cycles.

claims.claim: Only 167 workflows (2.78%) have a human-mediated path before an external action; 68.32% couple LLM output to external actions through logic or directly.
claims.evidence: BFS from LLM nodes to action nodes over a role-annotated graph (Table 6). Validation on 200 manually inspected workflows is reported only as 'confirmed ... correctly captured', with no accuracy or per-class numbers.

claims.claim: Only 684 of 6,003 workflows contain error handling that can be linked to LLM outputs, and it is mostly lightweight node-local configuration.
claims.evidence: Two-step anchor detection plus backward traversal (Tables 3-5): 1,123 of 5,383 anchors have an upstream LLM. The traversal heuristic is not validated against manual labels, and presence of a setting says nothing about whether it handles LLM failures at runtime.

claims.claim: Text generation (31.1%), information extraction and planning/agentic execution dominate LLM tasks in n8n.
claims.evidence: deepseek-v4-flash labels with 96% agreement on a 200-sample single-rater check; no inter-annotator agreement.

claims.claim: Explicit reliability mechanisms such as structured fallback paths, repair loops, failure-specific alerts and human approval gates are relatively uncommon.
claims.evidence: Only human approval gates (2.78%) and generic error anchors are quantified. Repair loops and structured fallback paths are never measured or defined in the body, and failure-specific alerts are only indirectly covered by error_trigger counts. The headline lists more than the analysis supports.

patterns.note: Describes how practitioners embed LLM nodes in developer-authored static workflow graphs (n8n). Purely descriptive: no runtime outcomes, no comparison of graph-structured vs free-form agents, and public templates are not production systems. Useful as a census of what static-graph users actually build, not as evidence that graphs help.
Human approval gates before external actions appear in 2.78% of templates; Takeaway 2 recommends approval nodes that also handle timeout and no-response cases. Prevalence only, no effect measured.

41.80% route LLM output through parse/validate/logic nodes before actions; Takeaway 5 notes such checks address format, not semantic correctness. 'Logic-gated' includes any control node, so it is not a policy guarantee.

methodology.sample: 6,003 public n8n templates (142,181 nodes); 200-workflow manual samples for RQ1 and RQ4 validation.
methodology.baselines: Keyword and NLI classifiers vs LLM annotation for RQ1 only; no baselines for structural findings.
methodology.models: deepseek-v4-flash as task annotator; templates themselves use many LLMs, not executed.
methodology.variance: n/a (census); no confidence intervals or inter-rater agreement.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint in journal template (Received/Accepted placeholders), no venue confirmed.
standards.artifacts: Scripts, identifiers and derived data promised 'upon acceptance'; current link is a Google Sites page, not an archival repository.

biases.detail: Public gallery templates skew toward tutorials and demos; the authors acknowledge production workflows are private, so prevalence of safeguards may be understated or overstated.
RQ4's 200-workflow manual audit reports no accuracy figure, and RQ3's LLM-linkage heuristic has no validation at all.
Static presence of nodes or settings is used to discuss reliability and safety, which are runtime properties; the paper concedes this for RQ4 but the abstract and takeaways do not.
Claims the first large-scale study of LLM workflows in low-code platforms, while concurrent work (2605.11229) already scanned 9,154 n8n templates for agent hijacking.
Data and analysis code are not yet released; promised on acceptance.

verdict_reason: A large, clearly scoped census with a validated task labeller and an honest threats-to-validity section. Validation for the structural and autonomy classifiers is unquantified, there are no runtime or outcome data, artifacts are unreleased, and the abstract's 'repair loops / fallback paths' headline is not measured.
applicability: For the DAG question this is a census of how people build static LLM workflow graphs, not evidence that such graphs improve results. Use it as a review checklist if the team builds n8n-style or code-defined workflow graphs for cross-repository work: (1) every LLM-to-external-action edge (write to a course store, publish, ticket, email) should pass through typed parsing and schema validation in a deterministic node; (2) approval nodes need explicit timeout, reject and no-response branches; (3) error handling should be an explicit graph path with an alert, not only node-local retry settings, which is what most public templates rely on; (4) format checks do not establish semantic correctness of extracted fields, so add source-grounded checks where accuracy matters. None of this is specific to graphs or to Java, and the paper gives no numbers on whether these practices change failure rates.

conflicts_with.detail: This paper treats logic-mediated LLM-to-action paths (41.80%) as containment. TaintAWI shows downstream workflow logic consuming agent output is the dominant injection channel (P2S 84.5% of confirmed GitHub Actions cases), so logic mediation without typed outputs is not a safety property.

JAW already analysed 9,154 n8n templates and found hijackable ones via chat-triggered SQL and shell nodes, undercutting the 'first large-scale study' claim, and shows that declared guards and human review can be bypassed (trigger synthesis, TOCTOU).
